[4, 7] The roadmap outlines four primary goals to be implemented between fiscal years 2024 and 2026: establishing CISA's role in OSS security, increasing visibility into OSS usage and risks, reducing risks to the federal government, and hardening the overall OSS ecosystem. [1, 4] CISA acknowledges that while OSS is a crucial driver of innovation and is foundational to technologies across the government and critical sectors, it can also introduce systemic risks through vulnerabilities and malicious attacks. [1, 2] This is the fourth iteration of the department's cyber strategy and it supersedes the 2018 version. [1, 2] It outlines four main lines of effort: defending the nation, preparing to fight and win the nation’s wars, protecting the cyber domain with allies and partners, and building enduring advantages in cyberspace. [2, 4] A key aspect of the strategy is the emphasis on working closely with allies and partners to build collective cyber resilience and capability. [1, 5] The document also draws on lessons learned from years of conducting cyber operations, including observations from the conflict in Ukraine, to shape its approach. [2, 4] Key consumer rights include the ability to access, correct, and delete their personal data, obtain a copy of it, and receive a list of third-party categories with whom their data has been shared. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On December 4, 2023, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added two actively exploited Apple vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog. [1] The flaws, identified as CVE-2023-42916 and CVE-2023-42917, affect Apple's WebKit browser engine. [1, 2] CVE-2023-42916 is an out-of-bounds read vulnerability that could lead to the disclosure of sensitive information, while CVE-2023-42917 is a memory corruption flaw that could allow for arbitrary code execution. [1, 3] Both vulnerabilities can be exploited if a user processes specially crafted web content. [2, 3] Due to the significant risk these vulnerabilities pose to the federal enterprise, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies were required by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01 to remediate them. [1] <2> Okta, an identity and access management company, experienced a significant security breach of its customer support system. The incident's timeline began with the initial compromise around September 28, 2023. One of Okta's customers, BeyondTrust, first detected the breach on October 2, 2023, and promptly notified Okta. Okta initially disclosed the breach on October 20, 2023, after confirming the intrusion on October 19. On November 29, 2023, the company announced that the scope was much larger than first understood, revealing that hackers had downloaded a report containing the names and email addresses of all users of its customer support system. The targeted facilities included a water treatment plant in Muleshoe, Texas, on January 18, 2024, and the Tipton Municipal Utilities in Indiana on April 19, 2024. [15, 11] The attackers manipulated Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs), causing equipment to exceed normal operating parameters, which resulted in a water tank overflowing in Muleshoe. [10, 15] In response, several U.S. government agencies, including CISA and the FBI, issued a joint advisory on May 1, 2024, warning operators about these unsophisticated but potentially disruptive attacks and recommending immediate security enhancements such as changing default passwords and implementing multi-factor authentication. [5, 7, 10] <2> On April 30, 2024, the White House issued National Security Memorandum 22 (NSM-22), a directive that replaces the 2013 Presidential Policy Directive 21 (PPD-21) to enhance the security and resilience of U.S. critical infrastructure. [1, 4, 5, 6, 8] NSM-22 clarifies federal agency responsibilities, designating the Department of Homeland Security to lead a "whole-of-government effort," with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) serving as the National Coordinator for Security and Resilience. [1, 3, 4, 6] The memorandum also directs the U.S. Intelligence Community to increase intelligence sharing with both government partners and private owners and operators of critical infrastructure. [3, 5] A key aspect of the new policy is a prioritized approach to risk management, which instructs federal agencies to establish minimum security and resilience requirements. [2, 4, 8] This marks a shift from previous voluntary approaches to a more regulated framework to address the modern threat landscape. [1, 8] <3> The Nebraska Data Privacy Act (NDPA) was signed into law by Governor Jim Pillen on April 17, 2024, and is scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2025. This act requires businesses that conduct business in Nebraska or produce products or services consumed by its residents to implement clear, documented privacy policies and robust data security measures. Key provisions include providing consumers with accessible privacy notices detailing data collection and sharing practices, and establishing strong administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect personal data from unauthorized access, loss, or misuse. The NDPA grants consumers rights to access, correct, and delete their personal data. [7] However, the implementation of these requirements into contracts is contingent on a separate, forthcoming rule (48 CFR) to amend the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS), which is anticipated by mid-2025. [7, 9] The DoD plans a phased rollout of CMMC requirements in contracts, set to begin in 2025 and achieve full implementation across all applicable DoD contracts by 2028. [2, 4] Since its emergence in February 2024, the RansomHub ransomware-as-a-service group has targeted numerous critical infrastructure sectors, including healthcare, water and wastewater systems, information technology, and government services. [4, 5, 6] The group employs a double-extortion model, encrypting files and exfiltrating data to pressure victims into paying a ransom. [4] According to the advisory, RansomHub had successfully victimized at least 210 organizations by August 2024. [4, 5]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The city of Mission, Texas, experienced a ransomware attack on February 28, 2025, that encrypted its entire computer network, including servers and backups, affecting all municipal departments. [8] This cyberattack severely disrupted city operations by making records such as police reports and personnel files inaccessible. [8] A significant impact was felt by the police department, whose officers lost access to mobile data terminals, preventing them from running license plate and driver's license checks through state databases. [4, 7] In response, Mayor Norie Gonzalez Garza issued a local disaster declaration on March 4, 2025. [3, 7] She also sent a letter to Texas Governor Greg Abbott requesting a state of emergency declaration to secure state assistance and resources to manage the crisis. [3, 6] The city engaged third-party cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement to investigate the breach and work on restoring the disabled systems. [5] [4] <2> The bipartisan 'Insure Cybersecurity Act of 2025' was reintroduced in the Senate by U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) and John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.). The bill mandates the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to form a working group. This group is tasked with analyzing and addressing issues within the cyber insurance market to develop information that improves communication about cybersecurity insurance coverage levels for issuers, agents, brokers, and customers. <3> On January 23, 2025, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued six Industrial Control Systems (ICS) advisories. [3, 10] These advisories detailed vulnerabilities in products utilized across multiple critical infrastructure sectors. [2, 10] The affected products included mySCADA myPRO Manager, Hitachi Energy's RTU500 Series, and several Schneider Electric products, namely the EVlink Home Smart and Schneider Charge, Easergy Studio, and EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody. [4, 10] An advisory was also released for the HMS Networks Ewon Flexy 202. [4, 10] The advisories provided information on security issues, vulnerabilities, and exploits to help users and administrators mitigate potential risks. [3] <4> On January 21, 2025, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued three Industrial Control Systems (ICS) advisories concerning vulnerabilities in products utilized across multiple critical infrastructure sectors. [2] The advisories addressed security flaws in a Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) II, Siemens SIMATIC S7-1200 CPUs, and ZF Roll Stability Support Plus (RSSPlus). [1, 6] For the TCAS II, used in aviation, the vulnerabilities (CVE-2024-9310, CVE-2024-11166) could allow an attacker to create fake aircraft on displays or disable collision avoidance advisories. [5, 6] The Siemens SIMATIC S7-1200 CPUs were found to have a cross-site request forgery vulnerability (CVE-2024-47100) that could let an attacker change the CPU's mode. [1, 6] The ZF Roll Stability Support Plus (RSSPlus), a vehicle safety system, had an authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-12054) that could permit an attacker to call diagnostic functions, potentially degrading system performance. [4, 9] <5> On January 16, 2025, the White House issued Executive Order 14144, titled 'Strengthening and Promoting Innovation in the Nation's Cybersecurity.' The order introduces several initiatives to enhance national cybersecurity. It expands the criteria for imposing sanctions on malicious cyber actors by amending Executive Order 13694 to explicitly include ransomware attacks. To secure the software supply chain, the order will mandate changes to the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), requiring software providers to attest to their secure development practices with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The order also aims to combat cybercrime and identity fraud by promoting the use of digital identity documents and creating pilot programs for real-time fraud alerts. Furthermore, it directs the Departments of Energy, Defense, and Homeland Security to establish pilot programs that leverage Artificial Intelligence for automated threat detection and vulnerability management. Finally, to improve the security of federal systems, the order mandates the adoption of phishing-resistant authentication measures like WebAuthn, directs CISA to deploy robust endpoint detection and response (EDR) capabilities across federal networks, and requires updates to FedRAMP cloud security guidelines. <6> The U.S. Treasury Department disclosed on December 30, 2024, that it had experienced a major cybersecurity breach attributed to Chinese state-sponsored hackers. [3, 4] The attackers exploited a third-party software provider, BeyondTrust, by gaining access to a compromised API key for its remote support tool. [3, 6] This allowed the hackers to remotely access several Treasury Department workstations and an undisclosed number of unclassified documents. [2, 3] The Treasury Department was first notified of the potential compromise by BeyondTrust on December 8, 2024. [5, 8] Following the notification, the department took the compromised service offline and engaged with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the FBI to investigate the incident. [3, 7] There is no evidence of continued access to Treasury systems by the threat actors. [3, 8] <7> Rhode Island's public benefits system, RIBridges, was the target of a major cybersecurity breach first detected on December 5, 2024. [4, 5, 6] The system, managed by the vendor Deloitte, was taken offline on December 13, 2024, after confirmation that hackers had infiltrated it and likely obtained files with personally identifiable information. [4, 5] The ransomware group Brain Cipher later claimed responsibility, threatening to release the stolen data unless a ransom was paid. [2, 10] The breach potentially exposed sensitive information—including names, Social Security numbers, and banking details—of approximately 644,000 to 650,000 individuals. [4, 7, 8] On December 30, 2024, it was announced that some of the stolen data had been released on the dark web after the ransom was not paid. [2, 10] <8> Black Hat USA 2025, a premier cybersecurity conference, will be held at the Mandalay Bay Convention Center in Las Vegas, offering both in-person and virtual participation options. The event features specialized cybersecurity trainings from August 2-5, followed by the two-day main conference on August 6-7, which includes expert briefings and a robust business hall. <9> The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has been notified that approximately 100 million individuals have received data breach notices related to the Change Healthcare ransomware attack, making it the largest known data breach of U.S. healthcare records. The cyberattack was detected on February 21, 2024, and was carried out by the ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware group. On October 22, 2024, Change Healthcare's parent company, UnitedHealth Group, officially informed the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) that it had sent out 100 million breach notifications. This figure confirmed earlier estimates that a substantial portion of the U.S. population was affected. The breach involved the theft of extensive personal, financial, and health data, including medical records, Social Security numbers, and insurance information. <10> On October 15, 2024, the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) published the final rule for its Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) 2.0 program, which officially became effective on December 16, 2024. [7, 8] This program mandates that defense contractors comply with specific cybersecurity standards to protect Federal Contract Information (FCI) and Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) as a condition for contract awards. [4] The rule, now codified as 32 C.F.R. part 170, establishes the CMMC framework. [7] However, the implementation of these requirements into contracts is contingent on a separate, forthcoming rule (48 CFR) to amend the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS), which is anticipated by mid-2025. [7, 9] The DoD plans a phased rollout of CMMC requirements in contracts, set to begin in 2025 and achieve full implementation across all applicable DoD contracts by 2028. [4, 9]
